Purpose

 Investigate and produce annual, summative assessment growth
 norms for SBAC ELA and Mathematics assessments.
 Investigate reporting metrics in use of results from growth norm
 results.

 issues related to misfit at LOSS/HOSS of assessment.
 Investigate properties of growth norms related to content areas and
 performance levels where students demonstrate low growth.

Why Growth Norms?

 The Smarter Balanced Assessment has a vertical/developmental
 scale allowing for cross grade comparisons of scores.
 The Smarter Balanced Assessment vertical scale allows for scale
 score gains to be calculated indicating magnitude of change for
 students from year to year.
 Gains are negatively correlated (-0.2 to -0.3) with initial status (larger
 gains for low achieving students) making interpretation difficult.
 Approximately 30 percent of gain scores are negative from 2017 to
 2018.
 Growth norms obviate this negative correlation phenomenon so that
 growth comparisons between students are meaningful.

Growth Norms

 “Growth norms" are most familiar to lay persons from pediatrics
 where height and weight norms are provided for children
 conditioning upon their sex and age.
 In education, norm-referenced tests have a long history with norms
 provided for students conditioning upon their grade and content area
 tested.
 Growth norms are calculated conditioning upon grade, content area
 and one or more prior achievement scores.
 Norms are often reported in terms of percentiles but can
 equivalently be reported as z-scores or normal curve equivalent
 (NCE) scores. For this study, percentiles, z-scores and NCE scores
 were calculated for student growth scores.

 Consortium wide growth norms were created for the following groups with
 associated N counts:

 (625,474), Grade 10 with Grade 8 as a prior (66,552), and
 Grade 11 with Grade 10 as a prior (12,566).

 Grades 3 & 4 as priors (654,041), Grade 6 with Grades 4
 & 5 as priors (636,687), Grade 7 with Grades 5 & 6 as
 priors (629,821), Grade 8 with Grades 6 & 7 as priors
 (625,221), Grade 10 with Grade 8 as a prior (27,881, and
 Grade 11 with Grade 10 as a prior (5,105).

Analytic Details

 Method 1:
 Quantile regression is used to model the complete distribution of the
 response variable (current achievement)
 B-spline smoothing is uses to accommodate non-linearity and
 heteroscedasticity of the data of the multivariate data.
 See Betebenner (2009) for more detail on the model used to create
 the growth norms.
 Measurement error corrected norms were also calculated as part of
 the comprehensive analysis of the data [Shang et al., 2015].

Analytic Details

 Method 2:
 Ordinal least squares (OLS) regression is used to model the
 distribution of the response variable using 1 or 2 priors.
 Residuals are calculated from the OLS conditional mean.
 Residuals can be reported in native scale score units, percentiles,
 standardized residuals, normal curve equivalents.

Analytic Fit & Results

 Method 1:
 All analyses converged yielding no analytic issues related to quantile
 regression estimation.
 With the exception of the Grade 11 growth norm calculations (where
 the number of students was small), model fit was extremely good for
 all norm-groups analyzed.
 Results showed variation among states that will be detailed in the
 final report.

Analytic Fit & Results

 Method 2:
 All analyses converged yielding no analytic issues related to OLS
 estimation.
 Model fit was generally good with consistent misfit at the low and
 high end of the distribution due to OLS assumption of multi-variate
 normality.
 Results showed variation amongst states that will be detailed in the

Conclusions
 Growth norm are used by several SBAC states.
 Smarter Balanced Assessments had suitable N-sizes,
 Deviations from multi-variate normality at the bottom/top of the
 distribution led to some misfit with procedures assuming a linear
 relationship.
 Several reporting metrics are possible for norms. Percentiles are the
 most frequently. Percentiles can be easily converted to scale score
 gains, standardized scores (z-scores), normal curve equivalents.
 From an interpretation perspective, percentiles are most broadly
 understood.
 Depending upon desired use cases, growth norms can also support
 criterion-referenced outcomes via growth-norm based projections.
 Depending upon desired use cases, growth norms can also be
 produced for within year interim assessments taking account of prior
 achievement and time lag between assessments.
